visual: Spectacular architectural shrub or small tree forming upright stems topped by enormous deeply lobed green leaves, often 60cm or more across and capable of approaching 1m in favourable conditions. New shoots and leaves carry pale brown felt-like hairs, with large sprays of creamy spherical flowers appearing in autumn on mature plants.
water: Water regularly while establishing and during prolonged dry spells. Established plants appreciate moisture during active summer growth but should not sit waterlogged through winter.
aspect: Best in full sun or very light partial shade in a warm, sheltered position protected from cold drying winds.
soil: Fertile, humus-rich, moist but well-drained loam or similar reasonably rich garden soil.
soilWarning: Avoid persistently waterlogged winter ground. Allow considerable space for underground spread because established plants can produce suckers well away from the original stem.
prune: Remove frost-damaged or unwanted stems in spring once new growth is visible. Unwanted suckers should be removed promptly if spread needs restricting.
toxicity: Fine hairs on young growth may irritate skin, eyes or airways in sensitive people; gloves are sensible when handling or cutting.
hardinessNote: Suitable for mild and sheltered UK gardens. Frost commonly removes the foliage and may kill stems back to ground level, but an established mulched root system can reshoot in spring.
resilience: Extremely vigorous once established in favourable conditions and capable of recovering strongly after frost damage, but the top growth is vulnerable to severe winter cold and exposed winds.
uses: Exotic gardens, architectural planting, jungle-style borders, sheltered courtyards and dramatic foliage displays.
uncertain: Final size and winter behaviour vary greatly with climate; plants may behave as large woody shrubs in mild sites or die back almost to ground level after colder winters.
Underground suckering can extend beyond the nominal canopy spread, so the displayed spread is not a containment limit.

visual: Ancient-looking evergreen tree fern with a thick fibrous brown trunk supporting a broad crown of gracefully arching, finely divided deep green fronds that can eventually reach around 2m or more in length.
water: Keep the fibrous trunk and root zone consistently moist through the growing season, particularly in warm dry weather. Water slowly around and onto the trunk so its surface roots remain hydrated.
aspect: Partial to full shade in a humid, sheltered position protected from drying winds and strong afternoon sun.
soil: Humus-rich, moisture-retentive but well-drained neutral to slightly acid soil with generous organic matter.
soilWarning: Do not allow the root zone or fibrous trunk to dry out. Equally, avoid stagnant winter water around the base.
prune: Remove old brown fronds close to the trunk once they have died. Do not cut or damage the central growing point.
compliance: Commercially harvested Australian tree ferns may be subject to source-country harvesting, tagging and trade controls. Dicksonia antarctica itself is not currently listed under CITES for trade restrictions.
hardinessNote: The crown is vulnerable below roughly -5°C. In much of the UK the crown should be packed with dry straw, fleece or similar insulation before significant frost, with extra protection around the upper trunk in colder areas.
resilience: Long-lived but extremely slow to form trunk. Healthy established plants tolerate cool damp conditions well but drought, drying wind and unprotected hard frost can cause major damage.
uses: Woodland gardens, shaded courtyards, exotic planting, fern gardens, sheltered containers and architectural focal points.
uncertain: Trunk growth is exceptionally slow, commonly around 2.5cm per year under UK garden conditions, so purchased trunk height largely determines the plant's apparent size for many years.
Fronds may be lost in colder winters even when the protected crown survives.

visual: Bold suckering deciduous shrub or small tree with thick spreading branches and distinctive reddish-brown young stems covered in velvety hairs. Large pinnate leaves turn spectacular scarlet, orange and crimson in autumn, while female plants may carry dense upright crimson fruiting heads.
water: Water while establishing; mature plants are reasonably drought tolerant once rooted and usually need supplementary watering only during prolonged dryness.
aspect: Full sun gives the strongest growth and best autumn colour.
soil: Highly adaptable to chalk, clay, loam or sand provided drainage is reasonable.
soilWarning: The underground root system can produce suckers several metres from the parent plant and may become troublesome in small gardens or close to paving and neighbouring borders.
prune: Little routine pruning is required. Remove unwanted suckers at their point of origin and remove damaged or badly placed stems during dormancy.
toxicity: Sap may irritate sensitive skin. Wear gloves when pruning or handling cut stems.
hardinessNote: Very hardy throughout the UK, tolerating severe winter cold once established.
resilience: Extremely tough, hardy and adaptable, with strong regenerative ability from its spreading root system. Control of suckers is usually a larger management issue than keeping the plant alive.
uses: Autumn-colour planting, large shrub borders, wildlife gardens, informal screens, banks and specimen planting where root spread can be accommodated.
uncertain: Plants are dioecious, so the conspicuous crimson fruiting heads are normally produced only by female plants after pollination.
Root suckers can extend beyond the nominal mature canopy spread.

visual: Compact clump-forming perennial with large glossy, strongly veined leaflets opening vivid reddish bronze in spring, becoming darker green through summer and colouring again in autumn. Tall red stems carry airy sprays of bright pink flowers in summer.
water: Keep consistently moist throughout spring and summer. Water deeply during dry spells because the large leaves quickly lose quality when the root zone dries.
aspect: Partial shade is ideal, though full sun is possible where the soil remains reliably moist and the site is not excessively hot.
soil: Deep, fertile, humus-rich clay or loam that remains moist but is not stagnant.
soilWarning: Dry soils and hot exposed positions can scorch and crisp the large foliage. Avoid planting where roots must compete heavily with established trees.
prune: Remove spent flower stems after flowering if desired and cut dead foliage to ground level after it collapses in autumn.
hardinessNote: Fully hardy through the UK once established; foliage dies down in winter while the crown remains dormant below ground.
resilience: Long-lived and dependable in consistently moist ground, but substantially less resilient to drought and hot dry exposure.
uses: Moist borders, woodland edges, pond margins, bog gardens and bold foliage planting.
uncertain: The current RHS accepted name is Rodgersia 'Bronze Peacock', rather than Rodgersia podophylla 'Bronze Peacock'.
The supplied shopping-list description gave cream flowers, but the cultivar is described by RHS as producing bright pink flowers.

visual: Bushy deciduous Knap Hill-type azalea producing rounded trusses packed with vivid rose-pink semi-double hose-in-hose flowers in late spring, followed later by attractive autumn foliage colour.
water: Keep evenly moist, particularly during establishment and while flower buds are developing. Water with rainwater where tap water is strongly alkaline.
aspect: Partial or dappled shade is ideal, although deciduous azaleas tolerate a brighter position than many evergreen rhododendrons if their roots remain cool and moist.
soil: Humus-rich, moist but well-drained acidic soil.
soilWarning: Ericaceous. Avoid chalky or strongly alkaline soil, which can cause chlorosis and poor growth. Use ericaceous compost for container culture.
prune: Little pruning is needed. Remove dead, damaged or badly placed wood after flowering and deadhead young plants if desired.
toxicity: All parts are harmful if eaten and can be toxic to people, pets and livestock.
hardinessNote: Very hardy in UK gardens, although an exposed position can damage flowers or developing buds.
resilience: Reliable and hardy where soil acidity and moisture are suitable; poor performance is most often associated with alkaline soil, drought or waterlogging.
uses: Woodland gardens, acid borders, spring displays, mixed shrub borders and large ericaceous containers.
uncertain: Ultimate dimensions vary with soil, climate and pruning; mature plants may gradually exceed typical garden-centre label dimensions.

visual: Bushy deciduous azalea with green oblong leaves that develop orange and red autumn colour. In late spring it carries masses of brilliant yellow funnel-shaped flowers with an exceptionally powerful sweet fragrance.
water: Maintain even moisture during establishment and dry weather, preferably using rainwater in hard-water districts.
aspect: Full sun to partial shade in a sheltered position.
soil: Moist but well-drained, humus-rich acidic loam or sandy soil.
soilWarning: Ericaceous. Avoid alkaline and chalky soils and do not allow container compost to dry completely.
prune: Normally requires little pruning beyond removing dead, damaged or badly placed branches after flowering.
toxicity: All parts are poisonous if eaten and are potentially dangerous to people, pets and livestock.
compliance: Listed in Schedule 9 Part II of the Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981 in England and Wales. Do not plant or otherwise cause this species to grow in the wild, and prevent garden material from escaping into natural habitats.
hardinessNote: Very hardy through the UK once established.
resilience: Hardy and vigorous in suitable acidic soil and capable of naturalising where conditions suit it, which is also the reason containment is important.
uses: Contained acid borders, woodland gardens and fragrant spring displays; unsuitable for planting where escape into semi-natural habitats is possible.
uncertain: Legal restrictions vary between UK jurisdictions; this compliance note specifically reflects its Schedule 9 status in England and Wales.

visual: Hardy evergreen palm forming a stout solitary trunk wrapped in coarse brown fibres and topped by a crown of large dark green fan-shaped leaves. Mature plants can carry arching sprays of yellow flowers and, on pollinated female plants, blue-black fruits.
water: Water regularly while establishing. Mature specimens are moderately drought tolerant but grow faster and look better with reliable summer moisture.
aspect: Full sun to light partial shade; protect from strong cold winds that can shred the broad leaves.
soil: Fertile, reasonably well-drained soil including loam and heavier clay where drainage is adequate.
soilWarning: Avoid stagnant water around the roots and very exposed windy positions, where foliage can become badly torn even though the plant itself survives.
prune: Remove only fully brown or damaged lower fronds, cutting cleanly close to the trunk without damaging living tissue.
hardinessNote: One of the most reliably hardy palms for UK gardens and capable of tolerating around -15°C or below in a sheltered position once established.
resilience: Exceptionally cold tolerant for a palm and adaptable to a broad range of UK soils, though leaf quality declines in severe wind exposure.
uses: Exotic gardens, architectural specimen planting, courtyards, urban gardens and large containers while young.
uncertain: Garden specimens are often sold and labelled at much smaller projected sizes, but old plants can eventually exceed 12m.

visual: Compact bushy evergreen palm usually forming several stems and a dense rounded crown of stiff green fan-shaped leaves. Mature specimens may produce small yellow flowers followed by date-like fruits.
water: Water regularly while establishing, then allow the upper soil to dry somewhat between waterings. Established plants cope well with summer dryness.
aspect: Full sun to partial shade in a warm position, ideally with some shelter from the coldest winds.
soil: Well-drained fertile loam or similarly free-draining soil.
soilWarning: Excellent drainage is especially important through winter. Avoid permanently wet heavy ground.
prune: Remove completely dead fronds as required. Do not cut into the central growing points.
toxicity: Leaf stalks can carry sharp spines capable of causing physical injury; site away from narrow paths and children's play areas.
hardinessNote: Hardier than its Mediterranean appearance suggests but less cold tolerant than Trachycarpus fortunei; severe UK winters can damage leaves or stems.
resilience: Wind, drought and coastal conditions are generally well tolerated once established, but prolonged severe frost and winter wet are the principal risks.
uses: Containers, gravel gardens, courtyards, coastal planting, exotic gardens and architectural displays.

visual: Dramatic evergreen or semi-evergreen subshrub with long blue-grey pinnate leaves made up of sharply toothed leaflets, creating an almost prehistoric silhouette. Mature plants may produce tall racemes of dark maroon tubular flowers above the foliage.
water: Provide regular moisture during active growth while allowing good drainage, then keep considerably drier through cold winter weather.
aspect: Full sun in a warm, sheltered position.
soil: Fertile, moist but well-drained soil with excellent winter drainage.
soilWarning: Cold wet soil greatly increases winter losses. In colder districts, a dry protective mulch around the root crown is useful.
prune: Remove frost-damaged stems in spring once the extent of dieback is clear. Plants may be cut back hard if winter damage has removed the top growth.
toxicity: Do not eat. Melianthus contains potentially toxic compounds and should be treated as an ornamental plant rather than an edible one.
hardinessNote: Top growth is vulnerable in cold UK winters. Established crowns often reshoot after moderate frost in sheltered gardens but require protection in colder areas.
resilience: Fast and vigorous in warm conditions but substantially less tolerant of hard frost and cold wet soil than many architectural shrubs.
uses: Exotic borders, architectural foliage, gravel gardens, large containers and sheltered courtyards.
uncertain: Foliage is often described as having a peanut-butter-like scent when bruised, but scent perception is subjective.
It may remain evergreen in frost-free conditions or behave almost herbaceously after colder winters.

visual: Bold evergreen perennial forming a substantial clump of long arching sword-shaped leaves with a striking metallic silver sheen. Small greenish flowers are inconspicuous, while female plants may later produce orange berries after pollination.
water: Keep moderately and consistently moist during establishment and dry summer weather, while maintaining free drainage around the crown.
aspect: Full sun to partial shade, ideally protected from severe cold and drying winter winds.
soil: Fertile, humus-rich, moist but well-drained soil.
soilWarning: Poor drainage around the crown can encourage rotting, particularly during cold wet winters.
prune: Remove individual damaged or dead leaves at the base. Avoid cutting the entire clump back unless frost damage makes renovation necessary.
hardinessNote: Best suited to mild or sheltered UK gardens. Severe frost and cold drying winds can damage or kill exposed foliage.
resilience: Tough in maritime and coastal situations where winters are mild, but significantly less dependable in cold inland gardens or persistently wet soil.
uses: Coastal gardens, architectural containers, modern planting, exotic borders and silver-foliage schemes.
uncertain: 'Silver Spear' is commonly encountered in trade, but RHS treats 'Silver Spear' as a synonym associated with Astelia chathamica rather than as the accepted cultivar name, so the accepted species name is used here.

visual: Graceful evergreen clump-forming bamboo with dense slender green culms and masses of narrow fresh-green leaves, creating a soft arching fountain of foliage rather than long invasive running canes.
water: Water regularly during establishment and dry summer weather. Container plants need especially consistent moisture.
aspect: Full sun to partial shade, preferably with protection from extreme drying winds.
soil: Fertile, humus-rich, moist but well-drained clay or loam.
soilWarning: Although clump-forming rather than aggressively running, an old clump still broadens gradually and requires adequate space.
prune: Remove dead, weak or badly placed culms at ground level and thin crowded mature clumps where necessary.
hardinessNote: Hardy across most UK gardens and substantially more cold tolerant than many ornamental bamboos.
resilience: Dependable, hardy and non-running, although drought and exposed drying wind can cause leaf rolling and scorch.
uses: Screening, hedging, containers, Japanese-style planting, evergreen structure and privacy planting.
uncertain: Fargesia rufa is commonly sold informally as an umbrella bamboo, but RHS uses dragon head bamboo; true umbrella bamboo is more commonly applied to Fargesia murielae.

visual: Tall elegant evergreen bamboo with feathery green foliage and upright culms that emerge green before progressively darkening through brown and purple to glossy near-black as they mature.
water: Water generously during establishment and prolonged dry weather, particularly in containers.
aspect: Full sun to partial shade in a reasonably sheltered position.
soil: Fertile, humus-rich, moist but well-drained soil.
soilWarning: Running bamboo. Rhizomes can travel beyond the intended clump, particularly in warm moist fertile ground. Use a properly installed rhizome barrier or a large robust container where containment matters.
prune: Remove weak, damaged and older crowded culms at ground level. Thin the lower foliage if the black stems are being grown as a display feature.
hardinessNote: Hardy through most UK gardens once established.
resilience: Strong-growing and hardy but potentially troublesome if rhizomes are allowed to escape containment.
uses: Screening, Japanese-style gardens, architectural planting, stem displays and large containers.
uncertain: New canes are green and generally develop their characteristic dark colour with age, so young nursery plants may have few genuinely black culms.
Rhizome spread can substantially exceed the displayed canopy width.

visual: Evergreen shrub or small tree with glossy leathery leaves and attractive reddish-brown shredding bark. Clusters of small white or pink-tinged urn-shaped flowers appear in autumn alongside round strawberry-like red fruits ripening from the previous year's flowers.
water: Water while establishing; mature plants tolerate considerable summer dryness once well rooted.
aspect: Full sun in a reasonably sheltered position.
soil: Well-drained loam, sand or chalk and unusually tolerant of lime for a member of the heather family.
soilWarning: Avoid persistently wet heavy soil, especially during winter.
prune: Requires little pruning. Remove dead, damaged or badly placed branches in spring and avoid unnecessary hard cutting.
toxicity: Ripe fruits are edible but are generally valued more as an ornamental feature than as a high-quality dessert fruit.
hardinessNote: Hardy in many UK gardens, particularly in mild, sheltered and coastal areas; young growth can be damaged by severe frost.
resilience: Evergreen, drought tolerant and notably useful in coastal conditions once established, but dislikes cold waterlogged ground.
uses: Coastal gardens, evergreen specimen planting, wildlife gardens, Mediterranean-style planting and small-tree displays.

visual: Large airy deciduous shrub with slender arching branches clothed in tiny scale-like grey-green leaves, becoming a haze of feathery pink flower panicles from late summer into autumn.
water: Water regularly while establishing; mature plants are drought tolerant and require little supplementary irrigation in normal UK conditions.
aspect: Full sun, with particularly good performance in open coastal situations.
soil: Adaptable to clay, loam and sand provided the site drains reasonably well.
soilWarning: Avoid shallow chalk and persistently waterlogged ground. Best flowering occurs in a bright open position.
prune: Prune in early spring before new growth, removing old or congested stems and shortening growth where a denser framework is required. It flowers on the current season's growth.
hardinessNote: Hardy through most of the UK, though young growth benefits from some protection from very cold drying winds inland.
resilience: Excellent tolerance of wind, salt exposure and summer drought once established, making it particularly valuable in difficult coastal gardens.
uses: Coastal planting, large shrub borders, exposed sunny gardens, informal screens and late-summer flowering displays.

visual: Dense evergreen shrub famous for brilliant scarlet-red new foliage that passes through pink and creamy tones before maturing to glossy green. Drooping panicles of small white lily-of-the-valley-like flowers appear in spring.
water: Keep evenly moist, especially when newly planted or container grown. Rainwater is preferable in hard-water districts.
aspect: Partial shade to sun, ideally sheltered from cold drying winds and harsh early-morning sun after frost.
soil: Humus-rich, moist but well-drained acidic soil.
soilWarning: Ericaceous. Avoid chalk and alkaline soils. Use ericaceous compost in containers and avoid prolonged drought.
prune: Normally needs little pruning. Remove spent flower clusters and damaged or badly placed shoots after flowering if required.
toxicity: All parts are harmful if eaten and potentially toxic to people and animals.
hardinessNote: Hardy across most of the UK, although young plants and fresh spring growth can be damaged in exposed frosty positions.
resilience: Long-lived in suitable acidic soil but vulnerable to chlorosis on alkaline ground, drought stress and pieris lacebug in some areas.
uses: Ericaceous borders, woodland gardens, spring foliage displays and containers.
uncertain: The current RHS accepted name is Pieris 'Forest Flame'; it is often sold in the trade as Pieris japonica 'Forest Flame'.

visual: Compact evergreen shrub with glossy dark green leaves and dense clusters of deep red flower buds held conspicuously through winter, opening to fragrant creamy-white flowers in early spring.
water: Keep evenly moist and do not allow containers to dry out severely.
aspect: Partial shade is ideal; avoid hot exposed full sun.
soil: Humus-rich, moist but well-drained acidic to neutral loam or sandy soil.
soilWarning: Often treated as ericaceous in cultivation. Strongly alkaline soil and intense sun can cause yellowing and poor growth.
prune: Little pruning is needed. Remove damaged or badly placed growth after flowering.
toxicity: Ornamental plant; do not eat any plant material.
hardinessNote: Hardy throughout most of the UK in a sheltered garden position.
resilience: Reliable evergreen shrub for shade and containers where moisture is consistent and soil is not strongly alkaline.
uses: Winter containers, shaded borders, woodland gardens, entrance planting and evergreen structure.
uncertain: 'Rubella' is a male cultivar and therefore does not itself produce the conspicuous berry crop associated with female skimmias.

visual: Dense evergreen shrub with small glossy dark green leaves and an exceptional spring display of rich cobalt to deep blue flower clusters opening from reddish-purple buds.
water: Water regularly while establishing, then reduce irrigation once well rooted. Mature plants dislike constantly wet ground.
aspect: Full sun in a warm, sheltered south- or west-facing position.
soil: Free-draining loam or sand of acid, neutral or alkaline reaction.
soilWarning: Winter wet is a major risk. Avoid poorly drained heavy ground and exposed frost pockets.
prune: Lightly trim immediately after flowering if necessary. Avoid cutting hard into old leafless wood because regeneration can be poor.
hardinessNote: Hardy in many UK gardens but vulnerable to severe frost, cold winds and wet winters; a warm sheltered site markedly improves reliability.
resilience: Fast and drought resistant once established, but ceanothus are not generally among the longest-lived shrubs and resent heavy pruning or waterlogged soil.
uses: Sunny walls, Mediterranean-style borders, pollinator planting, evergreen structure and blue-flowered specimen planting.
uncertain: Individual lifespan varies considerably with site and climate; 'short-lived' is a useful horticultural caution rather than a fixed lifespan.

visual: Robust deciduous shrub with arching stems, peeling older bark and deeply coloured purple-black three-lobed foliage. Rounded clusters of pink-budded white flowers appear in early summer, followed by reddish seedheads.
water: Water during establishment; mature plants are relatively tolerant of occasional drought.
aspect: Full sun for the darkest foliage, although partial shade is tolerated.
soil: Adaptable to clay, loam and sand in moist but well-drained conditions.
soilWarning: Very shallow chalk can lead to chlorosis despite the plant's otherwise broad soil tolerance.
prune: After flowering, remove selected older stems at the base where renewal is required. It also tolerates harder renovation if necessary.
hardinessNote: Exceptionally hardy and suitable for even very cold UK gardens.
resilience: One of the tougher dark-foliaged shrubs, tolerating cold, pruning and a broad range of soils with relatively few serious pest problems.
uses: Mixed shrub borders, dark foliage contrast, hedging, low-maintenance gardens and pollinator planting.

visual: Vigorous deciduous elder with exceptionally finely dissected purple-black foliage giving an acer-like lace effect. Broad heads of tiny pink flowers appear in summer and may be followed by purple-black berries.
water: Water while establishing. Once rooted it tolerates both relatively dry and fairly damp garden soils.
aspect: Full sun gives the deepest foliage colour, though partial shade is tolerated.
soil: Adaptable to most ordinary garden soils, including clay, loam and sand.
soilWarning: Very rich ground can encourage extremely vigorous growth, so allow sufficient room or plan to prune.
prune: For the largest and darkest juvenile foliage, plants can be cut back hard in early spring. Less severe pruning preserves a larger framework and gives more flowers and potential fruit.
toxicity: Leaves, stems and unripe fruit contain potentially harmful cyanogenic compounds. Flowers and properly prepared ripe berries are the traditionally used edible parts.
hardinessNote: Very hardy throughout the UK.
resilience: Fast, vigorous and adaptable, tolerating substantial pruning and a wide range of ordinary garden conditions.
uses: Dark foliage contrast, mixed borders, wildlife planting, informal hedging and pollinator gardens.
uncertain: Black Lace is the trade designation; 'Eva' is the cultivar denomination used in the accepted botanical name.
Hard coppicing improves foliage effect but reduces or delays flowering compared with lightly pruned plants.

visual: Compact rounded deciduous lilac with small dark green leaves and masses of fragrant lilac-pink flower panicles in late spring, packing classic lilac scent into a much smaller plant.
water: Water during establishment and during prolonged dry spells, particularly when grown in containers.
aspect: Full sun gives the best flowering.
soil: Fertile, moist but well-drained soil and particularly happy in neutral to alkaline conditions.
soilWarning: Avoid permanently wet ground or very acidic nutrient-poor soil.
prune: Remove faded flowerheads and lightly shape immediately after flowering if necessary. Avoid late-season pruning because it removes the following year's flower buds.
hardinessNote: Hardy through most UK gardens.
resilience: Compact, hardy and easy to maintain, with good tolerance of chalkier soils and urban conditions.
uses: Containers, small gardens, front gardens, scented planting, mixed borders and low informal hedges.

visual: Upright evergreen to semi-evergreen shrub carrying clusters of intensely fragrant pink-purple buds that open to pale pink and white flowers in the depths of winter, followed occasionally by dark berries.
water: Keep evenly moist while establishing and during prolonged drought, but never waterlog the roots.
aspect: Full sun to partial shade in a sheltered position where the winter fragrance can be appreciated.
soil: Fertile, humus-rich, moist but well-drained soil, tolerating neutral and moderately alkaline conditions.
soilWarning: Daphnes resent root disturbance and transplanting. Choose the planting position carefully and avoid repeatedly digging around the root system.
prune: Minimal pruning only. Remove dead or damaged shoots and make any essential shaping cuts immediately after flowering.
toxicity: All parts are harmful if eaten, with the berries particularly dangerous. Sap may also irritate skin.
hardinessNote: Generally hardy in sheltered UK gardens but flower buds and evergreen foliage can be damaged by severe cold or exposure.
resilience: Long-lived when left undisturbed in suitable soil, but notably intolerant of transplanting, severe root disturbance and waterlogging.
uses: Winter gardens, scented planting, entrances, paths, sheltered shrub borders and courtyard planting.
uncertain: Foliage retention varies with winter severity; colder sites may see greater leaf loss.

visual: Dense evergreen shrub with glossy dark green leaves and tiny creamy-white winter flowers that are visually modest but produce an extraordinarily strong sweet perfume, followed by shiny black berries.
water: Water during establishment; mature plants tolerate relatively dry shade but benefit from occasional deep watering during prolonged drought.
aspect: Partial to full shade and particularly useful beneath trees or on the shaded side of buildings.
soil: Humus-rich, moist but well-drained soil, though tolerant of a broad range of ordinary garden conditions.
soilWarning: Avoid prolonged waterlogging. Very dry root-filled ground beneath mature trees may need extra organic matter and establishment watering.
prune: Little pruning is needed; lightly trim after flowering or remove old congested stems if required.
toxicity: Berries are ornamental and should not be treated as edible.
hardinessNote: Hardy throughout most of the UK.
resilience: Exceptionally useful in difficult shaded situations and tolerant of increasingly dry conditions once established.
uses: Dry shade, woodland planting, winter fragrance, evergreen ground structure, shaded containers and planting near paths or doors.

visual: Dense thorny deciduous shrub producing brilliant deep crimson flowers with conspicuous golden-yellow stamens on largely bare branches in early spring, followed by aromatic yellow-green quince-like fruits.
water: Water during establishment; mature plants are reasonably tolerant of dry spells.
aspect: Full sun to partial shade, with strongest flowering and fruiting in good light.
soil: Very adaptable to chalk, clay, loam and sand provided drainage is reasonable.
soilWarning: Avoid permanently waterlogged ground. Thorny growth needs space away from narrow paths unless wall-trained.
prune: After flowering, shorten side shoots where wall-trained and remove congested or poorly placed stems. Avoid indiscriminate hard pruning if maximum flowering and fruiting are wanted.
toxicity: The hard aromatic fruit is commonly cooked for preserves; avoid eating the seeds.
hardinessNote: Very hardy throughout the UK.
resilience: Extremely tough, adaptable and tolerant of pruning, urban conditions and a broad range of soils.
uses: Wall training, hedging, spring flowering, thorny boundary planting, pollinator gardens and fruit for preserves.

visual: Large arching deciduous shrub whose graceful stems become smothered in masses of soft pink bell-shaped flowers with yellow-marked throats in late spring and early summer.
water: Water well during establishment; established shrubs need extra water mainly during prolonged drought.
aspect: Full sun to partial shade.
soil: Adaptable to most moist but well-drained garden soils.
soilWarning: Allow enough width for the naturally arching framework; crowding or constant clipping spoils its graceful habit.
prune: Immediately after flowering, remove some of the oldest flowered stems at the base to encourage replacement growth and retain an open arching structure.
hardinessNote: Very hardy in UK gardens.
resilience: Robust and easy to grow with few demanding requirements once established.
uses: Large shrub borders, cottage gardens, flowering screens, wildlife gardens and informal specimen planting.

visual: Low compact deciduous shrub forming a neat spreading mound of fresh green leaves, almost disappearing beneath masses of small pure white starry flowers in late spring before developing purplish autumn tones.
water: Water during establishment and prolonged dry spells.
aspect: Full sun to partial shade.
soil: Adaptable to chalk, clay, loam or sand in moist but well-drained conditions.
soilWarning: Avoid persistently waterlogged soil and very dry impoverished sites.
prune: If pruning is required, do it immediately after flowering and remove some older shoots at the base to encourage fresh flowering wood.
hardinessNote: Very hardy throughout the UK.
resilience: Dependable, hardy and relatively trouble-free, needing little intervention once established.
uses: Front of borders, small gardens, low flowering shrubs, containers and cottage gardens.

visual: Bushy deciduous shrub with lobed aromatic foliage and hanging clusters of rich crimson-red flowers in early spring, later sometimes followed by rounded blue-black fruits with a pale bloom.
water: Water during establishment; mature plants tolerate ordinary seasonal dry periods.
aspect: Full sun for the strongest flowering, though light shade is tolerated.
soil: Adaptable to chalk, clay, loam and sand provided drainage is reasonable.
soilWarning: Avoid prolonged waterlogging. The foliage has a distinctive pungent scent when handled that some customers dislike.
prune: After flowering, remove a proportion of older stems at ground level where renewal is needed and lightly shorten overlong shoots.
hardinessNote: Very hardy throughout the UK.
resilience: Tough, adaptable and reliable, with excellent early-season flowering even in relatively ordinary garden conditions.
uses: Early pollinator planting, mixed hedges, shrub borders, informal screens and cottage gardens.

visual: Dense evergreen shrub with large glossy leathery leaves dramatically splashed and spotted yellow-gold. Female plants can produce clusters of bright red berries when a compatible male aucuba grows nearby.
water: Water regularly while establishing; mature plants tolerate dry shade surprisingly well once rooted.
aspect: Partial to full shade, including difficult north-facing and tree-shaded positions.
soil: Adaptable to most reasonably drained garden soils.
soilWarning: Strong direct sun can scorch or bleach the foliage. Very dry shade beneath mature trees still requires careful watering during establishment.
prune: Prune or renovate in spring if needed, cutting overgrown stems back individually rather than shearing the large leaves.
toxicity: Berries are ornamental and should not be eaten.
hardinessNote: Hardy throughout most UK gardens.
resilience: Exceptionally useful for shade, urban conditions and root competition once established, with very low routine maintenance.
uses: Deep shade, evergreen screening, difficult dry borders, containers and foliage planting.
uncertain: 'Crotonifolia' is female, but a nearby male pollinator is normally required for reliable berry production.

visual: Slow-growing evergreen ericaceous shrub with glossy leaves and remarkable clusters of angular deep red flower buds opening into patterned pink cup-shaped flowers. The stamens are held under tension against the petals and spring forward when triggered by a visiting pollinator.
water: Keep evenly moist, especially during establishment and in containers. Rainwater is preferable where tap water is alkaline.
aspect: Partial shade to full sun where the soil stays cool and moist.
soil: Humus-rich, moist but well-drained acidic soil.
soilWarning: Strictly lime-hating. Avoid chalk and alkaline soil and use ericaceous compost in containers.
prune: Usually needs little pruning. Deadhead or lightly shape after flowering if required.
toxicity: All parts are highly poisonous if eaten and can be dangerous to people, pets and livestock.
hardinessNote: Hardy in most UK gardens provided roots are healthy and the plant is not exposed to severe drying winds.
resilience: Cold tolerant and long-lived but slow growing, with poor tolerance of alkaline soil, drought and root disturbance.
uses: Ericaceous borders, woodland gardens, specimen shrubs, containers and unusual flowering displays.
uncertain: Cultivar size is strongly influenced by age and site because Kalmia develops slowly and old plants may become substantially larger than typical nursery specimens.

visual: Elegant deciduous ericaceous shrub with a tiered branching habit and clusters of small waxy bell-shaped cream to pinkish flowers marked with red veins in late spring. The foliage later turns brilliant scarlet, orange and yellow in autumn.
water: Keep evenly moist, particularly while establishing and during dry summer weather.
aspect: Full sun to partial shade, sheltered from harsh drying winds.
soil: Humus-rich, moist but well-drained acidic to neutral soil.
soilWarning: Avoid strongly alkaline or chalky ground and prolonged drought.
prune: Needs little regular pruning. Remove damaged, crossing or unwanted stems after flowering.
hardinessNote: Very hardy in suitable soil throughout the UK.
resilience: Long-lived and cold hardy once established, but less tolerant of alkaline soils and summer drought.
uses: Woodland gardens, autumn-colour planting, ericaceous borders, Japanese-style gardens and specimen planting.

visual: Slow-growing deciduous shrub with rounded blue-green leaves and fragrant white bottlebrush flower spikes appearing on bare or newly emerging branches in spring, followed by exceptional mixtures of yellow, orange, red and purple foliage in autumn.
water: Keep consistently moist during establishment and dry weather.
aspect: Full sun to partial shade; good light improves autumn colour.
soil: Humus-rich, moist but well-drained acidic to neutral soil.
soilWarning: Avoid chalky alkaline soil and prolonged drought.
prune: Minimal pruning. Remove damaged or crossing branches after flowering if required.
hardinessNote: Hardy throughout most of the UK.
resilience: Generally healthy and long-lived in suitable acid to neutral soil, though slow-growing and less tolerant of drought or lime.
uses: Autumn-colour gardens, ericaceous borders, woodland edges, specimen planting and large containers.

visual: Elegant deciduous tree valued above all for exceptionally bright white peeling bark, which becomes increasingly striking as the stems mature. Green leaves turn yellow in autumn and catkins add spring interest.
water: Water thoroughly during establishment and prolonged dry periods, particularly on light soils.
aspect: Full sun to partial shade, ideally where low winter light can illuminate the white bark.
soil: Adaptable to most fertile, moist but well-drained soils.
soilWarning: Avoid prolonged drought and severely waterlogged ground. Mature size makes permanent container culture unsuitable.
prune: Prune only when necessary, preferably in late summer or early autumn; birches can bleed heavily if cut in late winter or spring.
hardinessNote: Exceptionally hardy and suitable throughout the UK.
resilience: Cold hardy and adaptable, though young trees need adequate moisture while their root system establishes.
uses: Winter bark displays, multi-stem specimens, avenues, contemporary gardens and mixed tree planting.
uncertain: The accepted RHS name uses subsp. jacquemontii rather than var. jacquemontii.
The bark becomes progressively whiter with maturity; young nursery plants may not yet show the full mature effect.

visual: Graceful large shrub or small multi-stem tree with bronze young foliage unfolding alongside clouds of white spring blossom, followed by red-purple edible berries and a final display of fiery orange-red autumn colour.
water: Water during establishment and prolonged dry periods, especially on light soils.
aspect: Full sun to partial shade.
soil: Moist but well-drained fertile soil, preferably acid to neutral and lime-free.
soilWarning: Avoid very shallow chalk and prolonged drought if strong autumn colour and healthy growth are expected.
prune: Little pruning is required. Remove dead, crossing or badly placed branches during dormancy and preserve the natural multi-stem form where possible.
toxicity: Ripe berries are edible and are also readily taken by birds.
hardinessNote: Exceptionally hardy throughout the UK.
resilience: Reliable, cold hardy and generally easy to establish where the soil is not strongly alkaline or drought-prone.
uses: Small gardens, multi-stem trees, wildlife planting, edible landscapes, spring blossom and autumn-colour schemes.

visual: Broad spreading deciduous tree or large multi-stem shrub with attractive flaking bark, curious clusters of crimson-red flowers appearing on bare branches in late winter, and foliage that can combine yellow, orange, scarlet and purple in autumn.
water: Water thoroughly while establishing; mature trees tolerate moderate summer dryness.
aspect: Full sun to partial shade; a sunny position usually gives the best autumn display.
soil: Adaptable to clay, loam and sand and unusually tolerant of lime, provided drainage is adequate.
soilWarning: Allow substantial eventual width; this naturally spreading tree can become broader than expected in confined gardens.
prune: Requires little routine pruning. Remove damaged or badly placed branches while young to establish the desired framework.
hardinessNote: Very hardy throughout UK gardens.
resilience: Long-lived, hardy and tolerant of a broad range of soils including lime, with generally low maintenance requirements.
uses: Autumn colour, multi-stem specimens, small to medium trees, winter interest and chalk-tolerant ornamental planting.

visual: Elegant deciduous tupelo selected for extraordinary autumn colour, when glossy green leaves ignite through brilliant orange, scarlet and crimson on a broadly conical tree.
water: Keep reliably moist during establishment and in extended dry weather.
aspect: Full sun to partial shade, with good light promoting the strongest autumn colour.
soil: Moist but well-drained, humus-rich acidic to neutral soil.
soilWarning: Lime intolerant. Avoid chalk, strongly alkaline soil and prolonged drought.
prune: Minimal pruning. Remove damaged or poorly positioned branches while young to establish a balanced framework.
hardinessNote: Hardy through most of the UK once established, provided soil and moisture requirements are met.
resilience: Cold tolerant and long-lived in acid, moisture-retentive soils but performs poorly on chalk or severely dry sites.
uses: Autumn-colour specimen tree, lawns, acid gardens, waterside planting and larger gardens.
uncertain: 'Wisley Bonfire' is a male selection, so ornamental fruit is not expected.

visual: Slow-growing deciduous small tree renowned for smooth cinnamon-brown bark that peels away in thin translucent papery curls, particularly dramatic when backlit by low winter sun. Three-part leaves develop brilliant orange and scarlet autumn colour.
water: Water regularly during establishment and prolonged dry spells.
aspect: Full sun to partial shade.
soil: Fertile, moist but well-drained acid to neutral soil.
soilWarning: Avoid severe drought and prolonged waterlogging. Strongly alkaline soil is less suitable.
prune: Prune only when necessary, preferably in late summer to minimise sap bleeding.
hardinessNote: Hardy through most UK gardens.
resilience: Long-lived and hardy once established but naturally slow growing, so major damage takes time to replace.
uses: Winter bark, autumn colour, specimen planting, small gardens and multi-season tree collections.

visual: Distinctive deciduous hazel with bizarrely twisted and corkscrewing branches, especially striking after leaf fall, plus hanging yellow catkins in late winter before the crumpled green foliage emerges.
water: Water during establishment; mature plants tolerate ordinary summer dry periods.
aspect: Full sun to partial shade.
soil: Adaptable to chalk, clay, loam and sand with reasonable drainage.
soilWarning: If the plant is grafted, straight-growing shoots arising from below the graft are rootstock suckers and can eventually overwhelm the twisted cultivar if left in place.
prune: Remove any straight rootstock suckers completely at their origin. Otherwise prune minimally, removing damaged or badly positioned growth while dormant.
toxicity: Nuts, when produced and fully mature, are edible.
hardinessNote: Very hardy throughout the UK.
resilience: Robust and adaptable, with the principal maintenance issue being removal of vigorous straight rootstock suckers on grafted plants.
uses: Winter structure, cut stems, specimen shrubs, wildlife gardens, containers and architectural planting.
uncertain: Not every plant encountered in cultivation is necessarily on the same rootstock, so the sucker warning applies specifically to grafted specimens.

visual: Compact ornamental crab apple with masses of white spring blossom opening from red-pink buds, followed by abundant small yellow-orange to orange-red fruits that can hang well into winter.
water: Water regularly while establishing and during prolonged drought.
aspect: Full sun for the strongest flowering and fruiting.
soil: Fertile, moisture-retentive but well-drained soil across a broad pH range.
soilWarning: Avoid severe waterlogging and extremely dry impoverished soil.
prune: Remove dead, damaged, diseased or crossing branches during winter. Avoid unnecessary hard pruning because it can stimulate excessive upright growth.
toxicity: Crab apples can be cooked for jelly and preserves. As with other apples, avoid eating substantial quantities of crushed seeds.
hardinessNote: Very hardy throughout the UK.
resilience: Dependable and adaptable, though normal apple problems such as scab, canker, aphids and mildew remain possible.
uses: Small ornamental trees, wildlife gardens, spring blossom, winter fruit, pollination support for many eating apples and preserves.
uncertain: 'Evereste' has a long flowering period and is a useful pollination partner for many apples, but calling any single crab apple a literally universal pollinator overstates compatibility.

visual: Distinctive small to medium deciduous tree with large pinnate leaves, airy panicles of bright yellow flowers in high summer and inflated papery lantern-like seed capsules that mature through bronze and brown.
water: Water while establishing. Older trees tolerate relatively dry conditions once well rooted.
aspect: Full sun in a warm, sheltered position.
soil: Well-drained chalk, clay, loam or sand with reasonable fertility.
soilWarning: Flowering and ripening are poorest in cold shaded sites. Avoid heavy stagnant winter soil.
prune: Minimal pruning. Remove damaged or badly placed branches during dormancy and establish a sound framework when young.
hardinessNote: Hardy through most of the UK but performs best with summer heat and shelter.
resilience: Once established it tolerates heat, urban conditions and periods of drought well, though young trees are less forgiving of severe exposure.
uses: Small tree specimens, urban gardens, drought-tolerant planting, summer flowering and unusual seed displays.

visual: Elegant open-crowned deciduous tree with fine fern-like foliage emerging brilliant golden yellow, maturing to light green and colouring yellow again in autumn. The airy canopy casts attractive dappled rather than dense shade.
water: Water thoroughly while establishing; mature trees tolerate periods of drought.
aspect: Full sun gives the brightest foliage colour.
soil: Adaptable to a wide range of well-drained garden soils.
soilWarning: Allow for the eventual tree canopy and root system; unsuitable as a permanent container plant.
prune: Minimal pruning. Remove damaged or crossing branches while young and maintain a clear structural framework.
hardinessNote: Very hardy throughout the UK.
resilience: Tolerant of urban air, heat and a broad range of soils once established, although young growth can be affected by gall midge and other occasional pests.
uses: Urban trees, light-canopy shade, lawn specimens, modern gardens and golden-foliage planting.
uncertain: 'Sunburst' belongs to the thornless form, f. inermis, and should not develop the formidable trunk thorns associated with typical Gleditsia triacanthos.

visual: Compact, bushier selection of cider gum with striking silver-blue juvenile leaves and pale stems. If allowed to mature into a tree, later foliage becomes longer and more lance-shaped; regular coppicing retains the highly prized round juvenile foliage.
water: Water well during establishment; once rooted, plants tolerate moderate drought but respond to summer moisture with stronger growth.
aspect: Full sun, ideally with shelter while young.
soil: Fertile, reasonably well-drained soil across a broad pH range.
soilWarning: Avoid stagnant wet ground. Even compact selections become substantial woody plants unless regularly managed.
prune: For juvenile cut foliage, coppice or pollard established plants in spring once frost risk has eased. Unpruned specimens can instead be trained as small trees.
toxicity: Eucalyptus foliage and concentrated eucalyptus oils are harmful if ingested in quantity and should be kept away from pets and children.
hardinessNote: Selected for improved hardiness and compact growth; established plants are hardy through most UK gardens, though young shoots can be damaged by severe frost.
resilience: Fast growing and strongly regenerative after pruning, with good cold tolerance for a eucalyptus but some vulnerability while newly planted.
uses: Silver foliage, cut foliage, specimen shrubs, small trees, contemporary planting and large containers with pruning.
uncertain: Azura is the trade designation and 'Cagire' is the cultivar denomination.
Ultimate size depends enormously on whether the plant is regularly coppiced or allowed to form a tree.

visual: Powerful deciduous climber famous for extraordinarily long hanging racemes of fragrant lilac-violet pea flowers in late spring and early summer, often displayed most effectively from pergolas and high supports.
water: Water regularly while establishing and during dry periods, especially before and during flowering.
aspect: Full sun is ideal for flowering, though partial shade is tolerated. A warm south- or west-facing position is particularly effective.
soil: Fertile, moist but well-drained soil across a broad range of soil types and pH.
soilWarning: Requires an extremely strong permanent support because old stems become heavy and woody.
prune: Prune twice yearly. In summer shorten long current-season side shoots to around five or six leaves, then in February shorten those same laterals to two or three buds to create flowering spurs.
toxicity: All parts are harmful if eaten, with the seeds and pods particularly poisonous.
hardinessNote: Very hardy once established, though spring flowers can be damaged by late frost.
resilience: Extremely vigorous and long-lived when established, but flowering quality depends on adequate sun, mature grafted material and correct pruning.
uses: Pergolas, arches, large walls, trained climbers and spectacular spring flowering.
uncertain: The accepted botanical name is Wisteria floribunda f. multijuga rather than the cultivar-style Wisteria floribunda 'Multijuga'.
Grafted named plants generally flower substantially sooner and more predictably than seed-raised wisterias.

visual: Glossy evergreen woody climber with dark green oval leaves that often bronze or redden in cold weather, carrying masses of intensely fragrant white pinwheel-shaped flowers through summer.
water: Water regularly while establishing and keep containers consistently moist during warm weather.
aspect: Warm sheltered full sun to light partial shade, ideally against a south- or west-facing wall.
soil: Fertile, humus-rich, moisture-retentive but free-draining soil.
soilWarning: Cold exposed sites and wet winter soil reduce reliability. Containers need protection from severe root freezing.
prune: Trim after flowering to keep growth within bounds and remove congested or damaged stems. Tie young shoots to supports until the framework establishes.
toxicity: Milky sap can irritate skin and the plant should not be eaten.
hardinessNote: Hardy in many sheltered UK gardens but vulnerable to severe frost and cold drying winds, particularly when young.
resilience: Dependable evergreen climber in warm sheltered gardens and increasingly tolerant of dryness once established, but exposure is its main limitation.
uses: Evergreen climber, scented walls, fences, pergolas, courtyards and large containers.

visual: Vigorous self-clinging evergreen ivy with exceptionally large leathery dark green leaves dramatically splashed through the centre with yellow and lime-green variegation. Mature flowering growth provides late-season nectar.
water: Water regularly while establishing; older plants tolerate considerable shade and moderate drought.
aspect: Full sun to partial or fairly deep shade, though leaf colour varies with light level.
soil: Adaptable to most fertile, humus-rich and reasonably drained garden soils.
soilWarning: Vigorous self-clinging growth requires management on buildings, gutters, roofs and vulnerable structures. Do not allow it to disappear into inaccessible masonry.
prune: Trim at almost any time to keep growth within its allotted area. Renovate overgrown plants progressively if necessary.
toxicity: Harmful if eaten and sap may cause skin irritation or allergic dermatitis. Also potentially harmful to pets.
hardinessNote: Hardy throughout most UK gardens.
resilience: Exceptionally robust, shade tolerant and drought resistant once established, though vigorous growth demands active containment on structures.
uses: Evergreen wall cover, shade, screening, wildlife habitat, late nectar and large containers.

visual: Vigorous twining climber with elegant leaves divided into five leaflets and clusters of unusual dark maroon-purple spring flowers with a sweet vanilla-chocolate-like fragrance. Successful cross-pollination can produce extraordinary purple sausage-shaped fruits.
water: Water regularly during establishment and prolonged drought.
aspect: Full sun to partial shade.
soil: Adaptable to most fertile, moist but well-drained soils.
soilWarning: Very vigorous once established and needs adequate support and space. Avoid planting where it can scramble unchecked into small shrubs or weak structures.
prune: Prune after flowering to contain growth and remove tangled or congested stems. More substantial renovation can be carried out where necessary.
toxicity: The soft pulp of fully ripe fruit is edible, though the plant is primarily ornamental and the seeds are not normally eaten.
hardinessNote: Very hardy in UK gardens, although foliage may be more deciduous in colder conditions.
resilience: Fast, vigorous and broadly adaptable, with strong regenerative growth after pruning.
uses: Pergolas, fences, scented climbers, wildlife gardens and unusual fruit displays.
uncertain: Reliable fruiting generally requires cross-pollination from a genetically different compatible plant, so simply planting two clonally identical specimens may not be sufficient.

visual: Twining deciduous honeysuckle producing long tubular flowers that are deep reddish-purple outside and creamy yellow within, followed by red berries. Its sweet fragrance becomes particularly noticeable during warm evenings when moth pollinators are active.
water: Keep evenly moist while establishing and during dry summers.
aspect: Full sun to partial shade; roots appreciate cool soil while flowering shoots perform best with good light.
soil: Fertile, humus-rich, moist but well-drained soil across a broad pH range.
soilWarning: Avoid severely dry impoverished soil and provide a support for the twining stems.
prune: Lightly prune after flowering to control size. Old congested plants can be renovated more strongly in late winter.
toxicity: Berries are harmful if eaten.
hardinessNote: Very hardy throughout the UK.
resilience: Strong-growing and cold hardy, although mildew and aphids can become more troublesome during dry or congested conditions.
uses: Wildlife gardens, moth planting, pergolas, fences, cottage gardens and evening-scented planting.

visual: Vigorous spreading hardy geranium forming a broad mound of deeply divided green foliage covered for months in large violet-blue flowers with darker purple veins and a small pale centre.
water: Water during establishment and prolonged drought; established plants tolerate ordinary short dry periods.
aspect: Full sun to partial shade.
soil: Adaptable to most reasonably fertile, moist but well-drained garden soils.
soilWarning: Very fertile soil or heavy shade can encourage lax sprawling growth.
prune: Shear or cut sprawling growth back during summer if needed; plants rapidly produce fresh foliage and another flush of flowers.
hardinessNote: Exceptionally hardy throughout the UK.
resilience: Long-flowering, hardy, vigorous and generally low maintenance, making it one of the most dependable modern hardy geraniums.
uses: Ground cover, borders, containers, cottage gardens, pollinator planting and long-season flowering.
uncertain: Rozanne is the trade designation and 'Gerwat' is the cultivar denomination.
The plant is sterile, which contributes to its exceptionally long flowering period because energy is not diverted into a normal seed crop.

visual: Bushy evergreen short-lived perennial with narrow grey-green leaves and upright racemes of purple-mauve flowers produced over an exceptionally long season, often from spring well into autumn and during mild winter spells.
water: Water while establishing; mature plants prefer relatively dry conditions and dislike constant irrigation.
aspect: Full sun.
soil: Well-drained chalk, loam or sandy soil of moderate fertility.
soilWarning: Excellent drainage is essential. Heavy wet winter soil shortens lifespan significantly.
prune: Lightly trim after major flowering flushes to maintain a compact shape, but avoid hard pruning into old leafless woody stems.
toxicity: Potentially harmful if eaten; grow as an ornamental rather than an edible plant.
hardinessNote: Generally hardy in well-drained UK gardens but severe cold and winter wet can shorten its life.
resilience: Exceptionally floriferous but naturally relatively short-lived, often declining after a few years; easy replacement from cuttings is therefore useful.
uses: Pollinator planting, gravel gardens, sunny borders, coastal gardens and containers.
uncertain: The often-quoted two- to three-year lifespan is not absolute; lifespan varies considerably with drainage, winter weather and pruning.

visual: Broad aromatic mound of soft grey-green foliage carrying masses of blue-violet flowers on branching stems from late spring through summer, with repeat flowering after cutting back.
water: Water while establishing; mature plants are drought tolerant once rooted.
aspect: Full sun for the best compact habit and strongest flowering, though partial shade is tolerated.
soil: Well-drained chalk, clay or loam of moderate fertility.
soilWarning: Rich wet soil encourages floppy growth. Leaner, freer-draining conditions generally produce a neater plant.
prune: Cut back after the first major flush of flowers to encourage fresh foliage and repeat bloom. An optional Chelsea chop in late May can produce a denser, later-flowering plant.
hardinessNote: Exceptionally hardy throughout the UK.
resilience: Hardy, drought tolerant, pollinator-friendly and generally very easy to maintain once established.
uses: Pollinator borders, path edging, cottage gardens, gravel planting, roses, containers and drought-tolerant schemes.
uncertain: Despite the name 'Walker's Low', the cultivar is not especially tiny and can approach around 60-90cm in favourable rich ground.

latin: Helleborus (Rodney Davey Marbled Group) Anna's Red ('Abcrd02')
visual: Clump-forming hellebore with leathery evergreen leaves intricately marbled cream and sometimes flushed pink when young. Strong stems carry outward-facing single rich red-purple flowers with contrasting cream stamens from late winter into spring.
water: Keep moderately moist and water during prolonged dry periods, especially in containers.
aspect: Partial shade is ideal, although full sun is tolerated where the soil remains sufficiently moist.
soil: Fertile, humus-rich, moist but well-drained chalk, clay, loam or sandy soil, favouring neutral to alkaline conditions.
soilWarning: Avoid stagnant winter water and severe summer drought. Container crowns should not remain permanently soggy.
prune: Remove old, damaged or badly spotted foliage in late winter as flower stems emerge, but retain healthy attractive marbled leaves. Remove spent flower stems later if seedlings are not wanted.
toxicity: All parts are harmful if eaten and sap may irritate skin; wear gloves when cutting foliage.
hardinessNote: Very hardy throughout the UK.
resilience: Long-lived, cold hardy and shade tolerant where drainage is good, although hellebore leaf spot, aphids and slugs can occasionally affect appearance.
uses: Winter containers, woodland edges, shaded borders, winter-flowering displays and underplanting deciduous shrubs.
uncertain: Anna's Red is the trade name associated with cultivar denomination 'Abcrd02' and belongs to the Rodney Davey Marbled Group/Frostkiss breeding series.
Blanket removal of every leaf in January is unnecessary for this strongly marbled evergreen selection; remove old or diseased foliage selectively.

visual: Graceful deciduous ornamental grass forming cascading mounds of narrow arching golden-yellow leaves striped with green, moving fluidly in the breeze and often developing reddish autumn tints before dying back.
water: Keep consistently moist during active growth and water containers regularly in warm weather.
aspect: Partial shade is ideal. Morning sun or gentle light improves colour, while intense hot sun can scorch and very deep shade reduces the golden effect.
soil: Fertile, humus-rich, moisture-retentive but well-drained soil.
soilWarning: Avoid severely dry sites and stagnant heavy soil. Plants emerge very late in spring, so do not assume a dormant clump has died.
prune: Leave the old foliage for winter protection and interest, then cut it close to ground level in late winter before new shoots begin emerging.
hardinessNote: Exceptionally hardy while dormant and suitable throughout the UK.
resilience: Long-lived and cold hardy where soil moisture is reliable, but growth is naturally slow to moderate and emergence is notably late in spring.
uses: Shade gardens, woodland edges, containers, path edging, Japanese-style planting and cascading over walls or raised beds.
uncertain: Spring emergence can be several weeks later than many neighbouring perennials, particularly after cold winters.
